## Why This Is Asked
Tests precise bit-twiddling without branches; validates wraparound understanding and constant-time composition.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation (circular shift)
- Modulo reduction via masking (k & 63)
- Safe right-shift with masking to avoid undefined behavior

## Code Example
```javascript
uint64_t rotateLeft64(uint64_t x, unsigned int k) {
  k &= 63;
  return (x << k) | (x >> ((64 - k) & 63));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you implement rotateRight64 using the same pattern?
- How would you vectorize this for an array of 64-bit words using SIMD intrinsics?

Why This Is Asked

- Uses bitwise complements and masks across two 64-bit chunks

- Bitwise masking on 128-bit structures
- Lane-wise composition without loops

function selectBits128(a, b, mask) {

}

// Implementation code for xor32 (C-like)

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates fundamental understanding of bitwise operations and rotation algorithms without using control flow, testing core computer architecture knowledge and low-level programming skills.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise shifts and their behavior with overflow
- Bit masking for input validation and range constraints
- Rotation invariants and proper edge case handling
- Branch-free optimization techniques
- Understanding of two's complement arithmetic at the bit level

## Code Example
```c
// rotateLeft32 implementation with no loops or conditionals
uint32_t rotateLeft32(uint32_t x, unsigned int r) {
    r &= 31;  // Mask to valid range
    return (x << r) | (x >> (32 - r));
}
```

## Interview Context
This problem tests candidates' ability to think at the bit level and implement efficient, branch-free code—skills essential for systems programming, embedded development, and performance-critical applications.

## Why This Is Asked
Evaluates ability to implement a branchless bit-reduction, a common low-level trick.

## Key Concepts
- XOR-fold reduction to a single bit.
- No loops, no intrinsics; width-generic approach possible.

## Code Example
```javascript
uint32 parity32(uint32 x) { x ^= x >> 16; x ^= x >> 8; x ^= x >> 4; x ^= x >> 2; x ^= x >> 1; return x & 1; }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt to 64-bit parity?
- Compare performance with a popcount-based approach.
